title: Two killed by gas explosion in apartment building in Russia’s North Caucasus
summary: Two more people were injured
text:
VLADIKAVKAZ, November 21. /TASS/. Two people were killed and two injured in a gas explosion that rocked an apartment building in Russia’s North Caucasus city of Vladikavkaz, the regional emergencies ministry department said.
The explosion occurred on the sixth floor of the building. Windows were smashed nearby, but no fire followed.
One of the victims is in critical condition.
The region's Investigative Committee branch said the likely cause of the blast was a gas leak.
A criminal investigation has been opened "over the ignition of household gas and subsequent structural damage to a residential apartment building" on charges of performing work or providing services that do not meet safety requirements.
The apartment was not officially connected to the gas supply, the city’s gas company Gazprom Mezhregiongaz Vladikavkaz said. Its owners have not opened a utility account, and the gas company has not carried out an official gas supply activation.

Wisconsin has also reported two deaths, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated death, involving a child.

text:

The Israeli military said several militant operatives were targeted in the area without providing further details. It did not immediately respond to questions on why it had hit a vehicle that appeared to be distributing aid.
World Central Kitchen did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The vehicle appeared to be carrying packaged foodstuffs, and papers inside carried the logo of World Central Kitchen, an aid organisation that distributes food in Gaza, according to a Reuters witness.
“It was just about to stop to distribute the food and drink to children when it was hit by a missile,” said Abu Zein Al-Daya, who also witnessed the strike.
Afterwards, meals of cooked rice were scattered around the vehicle, which was partially covered in the blood of the victims of the attack.

title: Retirees face a looming deadline for required withdrawals — missing it could trigger a tax penalty
summary: The busy holiday season may lead retirees to miss a key deadline for retirement account withdrawals.
text:
Every year, millions of Americans must take required withdrawals from retirement accounts by Dec. 31.
Amid the busy holiday season, it's easy to miss the year-end deadline for required minimum distributions — a mistake that can trigger a hefty IRS penalty, experts said.
"One of the most common RMD mistakes is waiting until the last minute," said certified financial planner Alex Canellopoulos, director of wealth at Vista Capital Partners in Portland, Oregon.
Most retirees must start RMDs from pretax accounts at age 73. The withdrawal is based on the previous year's account balances on Dec. 31, your age and an IRS "life expectancy factor."
The first annual RMD deadline is April 1 of the year after you turn 73, and future withdrawals are due by Dec. 31. If you wait until April 1 for the first one, you'll need two RMDs that year.
RMDs also apply to certain inherited IRAs if the original IRA owner reached RMD age before their death.

title: New fossil carnivore unearthed in the UAE – and named after Abu Dhabi
text:
A new carnivore species that lived about seven million years ago has been discovered at a fossil site in Al Dhafra region of Abu Dhabi – and the creature has been named after the emirate.
Known scientifically as Promegaviverra abudhabiensis, the creature, a type of civet, was identified from part of a jawbone discovered on Shuweihat Island about 265km west of Abu Dhabi city.
The animal, which may have weighed at least 20kg, represents an important link for scientists, as it provides evidence that giant civets migrated through ancient Arabia from Asia to Africa.
Palaeontologists at the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi who found the fossil have revealed details of the creature in a paper in the Fossil Record journal, co-written with a carnivore specialist who identified it as a new civet species at a Spanish university.
It is the first viverrid – a family of carnivores that includes civets and genets – found on the Arabian Peninsula.

Winter appears to have come early as the UK recorded its coldest night since January, with temperatures plummeting to below minus 10C in some areas.
Tulloch Bridge recorded a low of minus 10.6C in the chilly Scottish Highlands overnight on Friday, the second night in a row it was the coldest place in Britain.

PARIS, Nov 21 - The latest negotiating proposal for the European Union's next long-term budget is "deeply disappointing", the French presidency said on Saturday.
"It falls well short of what is needed, particularly on the Common Agricultural Policy, notably to guarantee income support for farmers," the presidency said in a statement.

MILAN/ROME, Nov 21 - Former Italian police chief Gianni De Gennaro, under investigation for alleged efforts to obstruct a new probe into the 1992 killing of a top anti-mafia magistrate, has taken his own life, an official familiar with the matter said on Saturday.
De Gennaro, 78, served as national police chief from 2000 to 2007. One of Italy's most influential security officials, he played a key role in the fight against organised crime, particularly the campaign against Sicily's Cosa Nostra mafia in the 1980s and 1990s.
Less than a week ago, prosecutors in Caltanissetta, Sicily, named him in an investigation of alleged attempts to obstruct inquiries into a 1992 car bombing in Palermo that killed anti-mafia magistrate Paolo Borsellino and five police escorts.
A judge had rejected prosecutors' request to place him under house arrest, but they appealed and a decision was expected in the coming weeks.

text:
Cape Town — Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa's first woman deputy president and a former United Nations under-secretary-general, has died at 71, the South African government announced on Friday.
Acting President Paul Mashatile conveyed condolences on behalf of President Cyril Ramaphosa, who is in the U.S., and said further details would be shared in consultation with the family.
A former anti-apartheid activist and member of parliament (MP), Mlambo-Ngcuka was deputy president from 2005 to 2008. She also served as minister of minerals and energy and as deputy minister of trade and industry.
She was in the first generation of MPs in South Africa's democratic Parliament, and sat in the Constitutional Assembly, which helped draft the country's democratic Constitution. Her time as deputy president was under President Thabo Mbeki.

title: Africa: Statement by the Secretary-General - on the Passing of Former UN Women Executive Director Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka
summary: [UN] I am deeply saddened by the passing of Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka. She was a lifelong champion of the rights and empowerment of women and girls.
text:
I am deeply saddened by the passing of Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka. She was a lifelong champion of the rights and empowerment of women and girls.
Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka’s fight began long before she entered the world stage. As a young teacher in KwaZulu-Natal and an activist against apartheid, she learned that freedom is never complete until it reaches every woman and every girl.
She carried that truth into history as South Africa’s first woman Deputy President (2005-2008), and for eight years, from 2013 to 2021, she carried it to every corner of the world as Executive Director of UN Women.
Most of all, Phumzile believed that gender equality is not a favour to be granted but a right to be claimed. She claimed it fearlessly and brought millions of women and girls with her.
On behalf of the United Nations family, I extend my deepest condolences to her family, to the Government and people of South Africa, and to the women and girls everywhere whose lives she touched and changed.
ai_summary: The UN Secretary-General issued a statement honoring the late Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka for her lifelong advocacy for women's rights and gender equality.

Seven people were killed in a clash between two tribes over the ownership of a forest in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, news agency PTI reported, quoting police Saturday.
The incident took place around 10pm local time on Thursday at Bilija forest in Battagram district, when armed members of the Gilal and Kaloch tribes confronted each other, leading to an exchange of gunfire.
According to police, armed men from the Kaloch tribe took positions and opened fire, prompting retaliation from the Gilal side. Four members of the Gilal tribe and three from the Kaloch tribe were killed in the clash.
The two tribes have been involved in a longstanding dispute over the ownership of Bilija forest, which has continued for several decades and claimed several lives in the past, police said.

This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.
The 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.
Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.

Four Strawberry Fields festivalgoers rushed to hospital after they were struck by lightning during wild weather
Four music festivalgoers have been rushed to hospital after they were struck by lightning at Strawberry Fields.
The group had been attending the festival on Friday at Tocumwal, on the New South Wales side of the Murray River border with Victoria.
A severe weather system passed through the area during the afternoon and into the night, causing acts to be paused several times as attendees looked for shelter.
Paramedics took two men to Shepparton Hospital in Victoria, according to ABC News, while a man and a woman, both aged 23, were taken to Deniliquin Hospital in NSW.

HANOI, Nov 21 - Vietnam's parliament approved a law on Saturday to speed up the expropriation of land in the case of some special projects, a move that could boost infrastructure development while reducing the leverage of farmers in fighting such seizures.
The legislation aims to ease delays to infrastructure and industrial projects in Vietnam, many of which have been held back by complaints from residents and farmers that compensation for expropriated land was below market value.
Under the revised land law, authorities may issue land-expropriation decisions before compensation plans are approved, provided no resettlement is required and the plans have been publicly disclosed.

text:
Washington is officially done with spending a pretty penny on penny production.
President Donald Trump on Friday signed the bipartisan Common Cents Act, which formally directs the federal government to stop minting the penny.
Both the House and the Senate passed the measure by voice vote, meaning no notable opposition.
“It costs nearly FOUR cents to make just one penny,” the bill’s author, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., said Sept. 29 on X a day after Senate passage. “This legislation will save $85 million per year by permanently ending penny production — it’s common sense!”
The U.S. Mint last year put the immediate annual savings of discontinuing penny production at $56 million.
The government stopped making pennies in November 2025, nine months after Trump called for the Treasury Department to stop production, writing at the time that the process was “so wasteful!” However, the U.S. Mint said it would still produce collector versions to be produced in “limited quantities.”

text:
Anger has never been allowed to belong to women. Exclusively the domain of masculinity (often segueing with bristling righteousness), anger, whenever associated with women, has historically, inevitably, been labelled “hysteria” and/or madness. An angry woman is an anomaly. She is ugly and unfeminine and irredeemable. In mythology, her anger makes her monstrous and in real life, her monstrosity is punished by the unholy trifecta of social exclusion, internet trolling, and physical violence.
It is this de-legitimisation of women’s anger that Nilanjana Bhowmick’s sharp new book, Why The World Needs Angry Women, counters. In 13 chapters, each of which centres on an angry woman who has chosen to channel her anger into change, Bhowmick writes a manifesto for our tediously patriarchal times. text:
A magnitude 6.9 earthquake shook the Andes in central Peru on Friday (November 20, 2026) with no immediate reports of damage or casualties.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the earthquake struck at 7:09 pm local time (0900 GMT Saturday). Its epicentre was in the Andes, 34 kilometres (21 miles) north of Junin, at a depth of 108 kilometres (67 miles).
Peru's Geophysical Institute said no damage or casualties had been reported. The earthquake was felt in the Peruvian capital, prompting residents to rush into the streets.
Peru lies along the "Ring of Fire", a 40,000-kilometre (25,000-mile) arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world's earthquakes occur.
In August, a 6.7 magnitude earthquake in the Peruvian Andes left two people injured and damaged several homes, health centres and schools, while in July, a 5.5-magnitude quake in the Junín region resulted in six deaths and 30 injuries.

Honda and Toyota both said there were no injuries or crashes tied to the vehicles being recalled, and there have been no airbag inflator ruptures. The automakers will replace the airbag inflators in the recalled vehicles.
There have, however, been at least 28 deaths in the United States and more than 400 injuries stemming from defective Takata airbag inflators since 2009, an issue prompting the largest auto recall in U.S. history. All of those deaths involved airbag inflators without a drying agent. At least 20 of those deaths were in Honda vehicles.

Freight train derails near Sejong, leaving Saemaeul, Mugunghwa services suspended
PYEONGTAEK/SEJONG, Nov. 21 (Yonhap) -- Five cars of a freight train derailed near the central administrative city of Sejong early Saturday, leaving Saemaeul and Mugunhwa train services between the cities of Daejong and Cheonan suspended. High-speed KTX services were unaffected, and no human casualties were reported.
The 21-car train went off the rails after an automatic emergency brake system activated as it entered Sojeong-ri Station in Sejong, some 120 kilometers south of Seoul, at 5:37 a.m.
When the train went off the tracks, it hit and broke a steel support pole, snapping the overhead power lines and causing a power outage between Cheonan and Jeonui stations.
The accident initially delayed Saemaeul and Mugunghwa passenger trains before services were suspended. KTX bullet trains, which run on separate tracks, were not affected.

The district of Katsushika seems typical of Tokyo’s unglamorous east side at first glance: a jumble of old and new shopping streets, narrow alleyways, a few gardens and temples. Aging workshops and factories show the area’s industrial roots. The Tokyo Detention House, which houses high-security inmates and execution facilities, looms along the Arakawa river.
It’s now the unlikely epicenter of a historic property boom that’s reshaping the Japanese capital.
Rents in Katsushika, one of Tokyo’s 23 wards, have surged 23.9% in five years, the most of anywhere in the city, according to a Bloomberg analysis of exclusive data from property portal estie. That comes after decades where prices barely budged throughout Japan’s long battle with deflation, and a renter could expect their housing costs to never rise.

title: Lancet retracts report by former SickKids pediatrician on infant’s death from opioid poisoning
summary: Lancet retracts report by former SickKids pediatrician on infant’s death from opioid poisoning Retraction Watch
text:
The Lancet has retracted a 20-year-old case report of an infant’s death by opioid poisoning via breast milk, following an institutional investigation that concluded the authors falsified the report by omitting key data.
The 2006 report described the death of a baby boy whose mother had been prescribed Tylenol with codeine, an opiate that gets metabolized to morphine in the body. The report’s first author, pharmacologist Gideon Koren of the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, used the case to claim for years that codeine, which gets metabolized to morphine in the body, can pose a lethal risk to breastfeeding infants.
That claim has been the subject of many articles in journals and the media, alongside scrutiny and investigations into Koren’s other work. In January, an article in the New Yorker brought renewed attention to Koren and the case report, and led a former Ph.D. student of Koren’s to come forward with new allegations about the case report. An expression of concern followed.
ai_summary: The Lancet retracted a 20-year-old case report on infant opioid poisoning after an investigation found the authors falsified data.

text:
The loneliness of modern life is a staple theme in contemporary Japanese cinema. Protagonists who long for connection but struggle with communication have become something of a cliche.
Yukiko Sode’s “All the Lovers in the Night,” based on Mieko Kawakami’s eponymous novel, centers on such a protagonist: Fuyuko Irie (Yukino Kishii), a 30-something freelance proofreader who works alone in her Tokyo apartment and barely speaks to anyone.
So far, so familiar. But working from her own script, Sode delivers a film of nuance and depth, both metaphorical and psychological. The US Treasury on Friday imposed sanctions on four Iranians who served as "oil trustees".

It's rare that investors get a chance to put a clear dollar value on a CEO.
With Jensen Huang, we just got one. And it's an astonishing number: $1 trillion.
That's how much Nvidia has lost in market value since Huang was forced out of the AI chip giant last week.
It's potentially a terrible look for Nvidia's board of directors.
After all, the fundamental job of a public company's board is to look after the interests of shareholders. That doesn't mean maximizing the stock price every day, or keeping a CEO at all costs. Directors have broader legal duties and sometimes must make difficult decisions that hurt investors in the short term.
But when a board oversees the departure of a CEO and shareholders subsequently lose $1 trillion, it's reasonable to ask whether the directors have fulfilled their most important responsibility.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that there was a "rumour" that Iran was building a dirty bomb. He added that if Iran was doing so, the United States would find out and stop it.
CNN had reported earlier this week that US intelligence indicated Iran could be attempting to build a dirty bomb and detonate it in Washington.
Iran's foreign ministry denied the allegations on Tuesday, calling them "baseless".
A dirty bomb is far less destructive than a nuclear bomb, which relies on a fission reaction.
Speaking to reporters, Trump also repeated his claim that the US has "total control" over the Strait of Hormuz.
"Last week, we took out record amounts of oil from the Hormuz Strait. Our navy has a blockade," he said. "We have total control over the Hormuz Strait."
"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, ever," he added.

‘Isla died of breast cancer at 17... her legacy could help other youngsters’
A teenager who died from breast cancer has lent her name to new guidance for GPs treating youngsters after a year-long campaign by her parents.
Isla Sneddon, from Airdrie, Lanarkshire, died in March 2025 at just 17 years old – two years after she went to the doctor with a lump in her breast.
Now her name has been adopted in new national guidelines to spell out four things GPs should keep in mind when treating a young person with unexplained symptoms.
Isla’s concerns were repeatedly dismissed as anxiety and hormones and her eventual referral was downgraded by the breast clinic from ‘urgent’ to ‘routine’ because of her age.
Her health deteriorated until she was diagnosed with a rare sarcoma which had spread to her heart, lungs and lymph nodes 24 months after first going to the doctor.
The teen’s grieving parents Mark and Michelle Sneddon said they hoped something good will now come out of their daughter’s death.

title: Nothing to Look At: What the Desert Might Do to a Tired Mind
summary: Nothing to Look At: What the Desert Might Do to a Tired Mind Vocal
text:
Nothing to Look At: What the Desert Might Do to a Tired Mind
Egypt's first monks went into the desert for silence. Psychology has spent forty years measuring what a walk in the park does to attention. It has barely tested the desert.
Some time in the fourth century, the bishop of Alexandria wrote a line about the Egyptian desert that still reads like a property developer's dream. "The desert was made a city by monks," Athanasius says in his Life of Antony. A young man from a village in Middle Egypt had given away his family's land and walked out to live alone. Others followed him, then many more, until by Antony's death in 356 the emptiness he went looking for was crowded with people looking for the same thing. The monastery that bears his name still stands at the foot of his mountain near the Red Sea, its church painted in the 1230s with warrior saints and long-bearded hermits that conservators cleaned of centuries of soot in the late 1990s.

text:
A study of 5,000-year-old skulls has shed grisly new light on what happened to some of the people buried alongside Egypt’s first kings.
Members of the royal households appear to have been killed when their king died, so they could follow him into the afterlife – a practice known as ‘retainer sacrifice’.
Almost 4 in 10 of the skulls show signs of potentially fatal blows to the head, according to research published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. The findings support a suspicion that archaeologists first raised a century ago but could never prove.

The post Ekiti Poll: Parties adopt final addresses before tribunal as Oyebanji urges dismissal of petitions appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria .
text:
Ekiti State Governor, Biodun Oyebanji, and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) on Friday asked the state Governorship Election Petitions Tribunal to dismiss the petitions filed by the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and the Action Alliance (AA) against the conduct of the 20 June governorship election.
Mr Oyebanji, the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate in the election, and INEC, which conducted the poll, maintained that the petitions are incompetent, full of defects, and constitute gross violations of the provisions of the Electoral Act 2026.
They stated this through their counsel before the three-member panel led by Abubakar Kutigi during the adoption of final written addresses by parties in the two separate petitions.
Mr Oyebanji, who was represented by his lead counsel, Onyechi Ikpeazu (SAN), argued that the petitioners (SDP and AA) have not proved that his return as governor was invalid by reason of non-compliance with the provisions of the Electoral Act 2026.
ai_summary: Governor Biodun Oyebanji and INEC have requested the dismissal of election petitions challenging the results of the Ekiti State governorship election.

title: SIIPS Report: Nigeria’s payment system retains status as Africa’s only “mature” system
summary: Last year, Nigeria’s NIP became the first and only instant payment system in Africa to attain mature status, during the launch of the 2025 edition of the report in Eswatini. The post SIIPS Report: Nigeria’s payment system retains status as Africa’s only “mature” system appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria .
text:
Nigeria’s National Instant Payment (NIP) system has retained its status as the only “mature” instant payment system (IPS) in Africa, according to the 2026 State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems (SIIPS) report released on Thursday.
The SIIPS report is an annual flagship publication of the AfricaNenda Foundation that assesses the inclusivity of instant payment systems across the continent.
Instant payment systems are open-loop retail payment platforms that enable irrevocable, low-value digital credit transactions in near real time, 24 hours a day, year-round.
The report assesses all operational instant payment systems annually and classifies them into four categories based on their level of inclusivity: unranked, basic, progressed and mature.
Last year, Nigeria’s NIP became the first and only instant payment system in Africa to attain the mature status, during the launch of the 2025 edition of the report in Eswatini.

ai_summary: Nigeria's National Instant Payment system has maintained its status as the only mature instant payment system in Africa according to a new report.

title: Russia’s Changing Positions on North Korea Sanctions and Denuclearization
summary: Russia once held firm on denuclearization and reluctantly accepted sanctions as a necessary tool. Those days are over.
text:
In recent years, Moscow’s official stance on North Korea’s denuclearization and sanctions has shifted: Russian diplomats now say denuclearization has become an irrelevant term and sanctions have proved ineffective. Both issues became part of Russia’s broader criticism of the United States’ policy.
Moscow’s skepticism of sanctions dates back to the 2000s. During the Six-Party Talks in 2003-2009, Russia argued that sanctions should persuade North Korea to maintain dialogue rather than punish it. After Pyongyang announced its exit from the Six-Party Talks in April 2009, Russia’s then-Vice Foreign Minister Alexey Borodavkin claimed participants would be better off discussing how to resume the multilateral format than strengthening sanctions.
When United Nations sanctions were tightened following North Korea’s second nuclear test in May 2010, Russia’s permanent representatives to the U.N. highlighted that the measures should not have negative humanitarian consequences and could be reversed
ai_summary: Russia has shifted its official stance on North Korea, increasingly viewing sanctions as ineffective and denuclearization as an outdated policy goal.

title: Vietnam narrows death penalty to four crimes, drops drug trafficking from list
text:
Vietnam has narrowed the use of capital punishment to just four crimes under a revised penal code passed by the National Assembly on Friday.
The death sentence will now be reserved for treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production. Drug trafficking, crimes against humanity, war crimes, rebellion and the rape of a juvenile have been removed from the list of offences punishable by death, with life imprisonment becoming the maximum sentence for these crimes.
The move marks another step in Vietnam's gradual reduction of capital offences. The country's 1985 penal code had listed 44 crimes that could attract the death penalty.
The decision comes despite reservations among some lawmakers about removing capital punishment for drug trafficking, a serious offence in the Southeast Asian country.

title: Is having debt actually bad?

“Debt isn’t inherently bad,” says finance coach and chartered accountant Carol Glynn. “Having debt doesn’t mean you have failed financially. What matters is the purpose behind the debt and why you’re using it.”
Steve Cronin, financial adviser and founder of Dead Simple Saving, frames his response in straightforward economic terms. “There is cheap debt like mortgages and car loans, then there is expensive debt like personal loans and credit card debt. Expensive debt is bad and can ruin your life. Cheap debt is fine and can help you get ahead in life, as long as you can afford the monthly payments.”

title: Arabic word of the week: How 'bahr' connects the sea, Bahrain and poetry
text:
A sea, a country and the rhythm of a poem all share the meaning of our Arabic word of the week.
Bahr means “sea”, as in Al Bahr al-Ahmar, the Red Sea. It also appears in Bahrain, meaning “the two seas”. The Gulf country’s Ministry of Transportation links the name to freshwater springs found in the surrounding salt water.
That coastal term stems from the root letters ba, ha and ra.
Abhara means “to sail”, while a bahhar is a sailor. The plural bihar means “seas”.
The depth and waves of the ocean give rise to metaphors that reach into spirituality and literature.
In Surat Al Kahf, the Quran turns the metaphor of the sea’s seeming vastness around, showing how limited it is in comparison with the depth and richness of God’s words: “The sea would be used up before the words of my Lord were exhausted.”

Yemen’s Houthis said on Friday that they had attacked a power station in Saudi Arabia’s Al-Shuqaiq and the port of Jizan, in response to Saudi-led coalition strikes on Yemen.

US tech sell-off continues as Anthropic tumbles after mega IPO
Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing but that was not the case on Friday.
Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street has fizzled out a day later, as a dramatic unravelling of the artificial intelligence trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.
On Friday, the stock, the biggest public stock offering ever and which surpassed $2 trillion in value at one point, was trading at $87.95, about 9.5 percent down from Thursday’s close, at about 11:30am in New York (16:30 GMT).
Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing after a turbulent stretch. text:
Two men have been killed after their glider crashed into Loch Leven, a large body of water in Perth and Kinross, on Friday morning.
Police Scotland said their bodies were recovered from the loch by the emergency services after the alarm was raised at 11.05am on Friday.
The force said next of kin had been told and the incident was not being treated as suspicious. Two Coastguard helicopters and an air ambulance were sent to the scene, along with a fire service appliance and a specialist crew.
The pair had flown off from the Scottish Gliding Centre at Portmoak airfield near the loch’s eastern shore in a Perkoz two-person glider on a training flight.
A spokesperson for the gliding centre said: “The incident is currently under investigation by air accident investigation branch of the Department for Transport and the police in conjunction with the British Gliding Association.

text:
'Iranians are after me': US Treasury secretary says he lives on a military base
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that he was still living on a US military base after receiving unspecified threats from Iran, but vowed to keep squeezing the country economically.
"The Iranians are after me. I'm not going to be cowered by the Iranians. Life on the military base is good," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC.
"If the Iranians are after me, it means that they are being squeezed. We're going to continue squeezing them," he added.
The US Treasury has been tightening sanctions on Iran since the US and Israel launched strikes on the country in February.
"Operation Economic Outcast, which we are two and a half months into, is the greatest economic isolation of any country in history," Bessent said.
"For the first time in history since Iran started producing oil, they have no oil on the water, so there is no crude for anyone to buy. No Iranian crude for anyone to buy."

ai_summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated he is living on a military base due to threats from Iran while vowing to continue strict economic sanctions against the country.

text:
The Deputy Vice-Chancellor for Research, Innovation and Enterprise at the University of Kigali, Rwanda, Professor Ogechi Adeola, has outlined a seven-point agenda for the renewal of the South-East, urging leaders and stakeholders to address insecurity, promote inclusive dialogue and turn the region’s human and economic resources into measurable development.
Adeola said the resilience of the Igbo people should not be celebrated as a substitute for addressing the conditions that make survival difficult, including insecurity, disrupted livelihoods and inadequate systems.

Asked about the damage, Khusnullin said the main girder of the arch span and the arch itself had been damaged. He said the authorities have two options for restoring the bridge.
A day earlier, Khusnullin said officials were weighing three options based on how much each would cost and how long it would take. He also said some parts of the bridge could reopen in a month or two.

title: Somalia: UAE Condemns What It Calls Somalia's Escalating Hostile Conduct
summary: [Shabelle] Abu Dhabi -- The United Arab Emirates has strongly condemned what it described as increasingly hostile conduct by the Somali government, saying recent actions threaten diplomatic relations and cooperation between the two countries.
text:
Abu Dhabi — The United Arab Emirates has strongly condemned what it described as increasingly hostile conduct by the Somali government, saying recent actions threaten diplomatic relations and cooperation between the two countries.
In a statement, the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs said decisions affecting bilateral relations should be guided by shared interests and kept separate from political considerations and domestic disputes.
The ministry also expressed concern over what it described as Somalia's attempt to bring internal disagreements over power-sharing into relations between the two countries, warning that such developments could negatively affect the interests of their two brotherly peoples.
The UAE said it closed its embassy in Mogadishu and withdrew its diplomatic staff from Somalia in January 2026, citing actions by the Somali government, including decisions to terminate bilateral agreements between the two countries.

text:
Dutch national Jan Willem Akster has been found guilty of five counts of sodomy by the Chief Resident Magistrate's Court in Blantyre, ending a case that has run for more than six years.
Chief Resident Magistrate Paul Chiotcha delivered the judgment on Friday morning. The court has revoked Akster's bail and ordered that he be remanded in custody pending sentencing. The sentencing date is yet to be announced.
Akster was accused of sexually abusing boys in return for bursary benefits he managed as finance director of the Timotheos Foundation, the development arm of the Reformed Presbyterian Church of Malawi.
He came to Malawi in 2011 to help run the foundation, which was set up on June 10, 2011, to promote Christian evangelism and support vulnerable children, mainly through education bursaries. He rose to become a senior figure, overseeing its finances and bursary programme. When he left the foundation in 2019, he claimed its assets were close to US$2 million.

The 2026 midterm elections produced a major political shift in Washington. Democrats will control both chambers of Congress when the new session begins in January, during President Donald Trump’s final two years in the White House.
That combination almost guarantees more conflict over energy policy, but it does not necessarily mean sweeping changes in federal law. The more consequential changes may occur somewhere else.
Governors, state legislatures, and utility commissions have substantial authority over where power plants and transmission lines are built, what utilities can charge customers, how large new electricity users are treated, and how environmental and water permits are issued. The election changed control of several of those institutions, including in states experiencing rapid growth in electricity demand. As a result, the most important energy-policy consequences of the midterms may emerge state by state rather than through another major act of Congress.

text:
The Red Command (Comando Vermelho – CV) is Brazil’s oldest criminal group. Created in a Rio de Janeiro prison in the 1970s as a self-protection group for prisoners, it started out with low-level crimes like muggings and bank robberies. But in the 1980s, the group moved into the cocaine trade, working with Colombian drug cartels and taking on a social leadership role in many of Rio’s marginalized neighborhoods.
It has since grown into a sizable national and transnational threat. War on Iran leaves Arab monarchies facing $1 trillion in losses
TEHRAN — The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran will cost the six Arab monarchies in the Persian Gulf nearly $1 trillion in destroyed infrastructure and lost economic output through 2030, Allianz Research estimates, leaving governments to borrow heavily and redirect wealth once invested abroad toward repairs and protection at home.
Its November report projects $790 billion in output losses over 2026–30, alongside just over $200 billion in physical damage.
The output figure measures the gap against the prewar growth trajectory. More than 80 energy facilities have been hit, about one-third severely, although most production infrastructure escaped major damage.
Geography determines who suffers most. Allianz forecasts a 4% contraction across the Persian Gulf Cooperation Council this year, with Hormuz-dependent Qatar shrinking 14%, Kuwait 11% and Bahrain 8%.

If you use the same stones from centuries-old monuments to build your home, does that make your home a centuries-old monument? This question might come to mind while reading further.

Sometimes, these stones carry fragments of a history that the people using them may not even know about. What appears to be an ordinary piece of building material could once have belonged to a temple, a public monument or even an imperial structure.

  Jakarta: Wildfires that tore through Indonesian forest and peatland areas this year could cost the Southeast Asian country more than $30 billion, the co-author of a study on the subject said on Friday.

The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years.
Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.
A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.
The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.
UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.
Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.

“The EU must be clear that it cannot join consensus on a package that would represent a substantive step backwards for global climate action,” Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra and Irish Climate minister Darragh O’Brien wrote on behalf of the EU’s 27 member states.

Chinese rulers already recognized the importance of accurate population data more than 3,000 years ago. Under the Western Zhou dynasty, officials presented the king with such figures in an annual ritual honoring the star believed to govern population counts.

Lagner and Lisa Herrold each sat at 3,162 votes after Duval County's Supervisor of Elections Jerry Holland initiated both a manual and a machine recount.
The deadlock initiated the unique tiebreaker last week in which each candidate would have the chance to win two of three coin flips.
Under the city's election rules, each candidate had a chance to call the coin's landing. Herrold went first, calling heads, but the coin landed tails, giving Lagner a 1-0 lead.

title: Diplomat calls on OSCE to condemn discrimination against Russian athletes
summary: Dmitry Polyansky noted that Moscow had long observed growing efforts by several OSCE participating States to politicize sports
text:
VIENNA, November 20. /TASS/. Russia’s Permanent Representative to the OSCE Dmitry Polyansky has called on the organization's leadership to condemn discrimination against Russian athletes by several participating states.
"We strongly urge the heads of the relevant executive structures to respond to these developments and issue a clear public assessment of the discriminatory measures targeting our athletes. Quiet diplomacy alone will not suffice," the diplomat said at a meeting of the OSCE Permanent Council.
He noted that Moscow had long observed growing efforts by several OSCE participating States to politicize sports. These efforts have resulted in violations of the rights of athletes from countries that have fallen out of favor with the West.
"OSCE participating States must take concrete steps to protect athletes, including athletes with disabilities and minors, if they are genuinely committed to ensuring that sports remain impartial and unbiased," Polyansky said.

Speaking random words like “cat” and “box” into her phone while filming herself in her pyjamas, Amy Butterworth’s relentless search for a job had reached a new level of absurdity.
The 19-year-old from Blackpool was applying for a role at Marks & Spencer, but first had to prove she was not a robot.
After downloading an app, filming her face from different angles, speaking particular words, inputting numbers and sharing a picture of her passport, she eventually received an email offering interview slots.
Yet within two minutes of the message arriving, all the slots were gone. In the small print, the retailer admitted it could not promise an interview to everybody offered one. “I just felt kind of stupid,” Butterworth said.
This is the demoralising reality for many young people in Blackpool, where more than one in five 16- to 24-year-olds are out of work and education, the highest proportion in England.

US President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a historic meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen that delivered modest wins for all three men but no game-changing accords.

The discovery, announced on November 18 by Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, was made by archaeologists from the Supreme Council of Antiquities.
Hundreds of stone sarcophagi were found in the upper archaeological layer, some damaged by looting and stone quarrying in the past. Terracotta sarcophagi, remains of wooden coffins and vaulted mudbrick tombs were also uncovered.
Some of the sarcophagi are anthropoid, or human-shaped, while others are decorated with images featuring exaggerated facial characteristics. This variety suggests that different burial traditions were practised at the necropolis.

“China has already begun construction of a dam in Medog County, around 40 km from the border… without consulting us or sharing any information,” warned Chief Minister Pema Khandu of Arunachal Pradesh. He called China’s $167 billion mega-dam in a seismically active zone an existential potential “water bomb.”
The Medog dam is not an isolated incident. It’s just one sign of a larger crisis extending across Asia’s river basins, where downstream nations face upper-riparian infrastructure that proceeds unilaterally, without environmental impact disclosures, binding legal frameworks, or genuine transboundary consultation and governance.

title: Russia Has No Timeline for Crimean Bridge Repairs, Deputy PM Says
summary: Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin said both the steel arch and the main beam supporting the roadway were damaged in this week's Ukrainian strikes.
text:
Russia has yet to determine how long it will take to repair the Crimean Bridge after a Ukrainian strike brought down its main road span this week, Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin said Friday.
The bridge, which links southern Russia to annexed Crimea across the Kerch Strait, remains closed to road traffic, while train service has partially resumed on a single track on the adjacent rail span.
“Our designers are calculating,” Khusnullin told state media, adding that officials would be able to give a timeline once engineers finished drawing up repair plans.
He said both the steel arch and the main beam supporting the roadway had been damaged.
Ukrainian drones and missiles brought down the central road span on Tuesday in one of three attacks on the bridge this week that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described as retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed to respond with greater force.

title: Myanmar genocide ruling: Rohingya say struggle for justice not over
summary: The ICJ held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya and ordered restitution and reparations. Members of the community hailed the ruling but cautioned that achieving real change would be long and difficult.
text:
Myanmar genocide ruling: Rohingya say struggle for justice not over
November 20, 2026
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the country's Rohingya community a decade ago, in a historic judgment hailed by the long-persecuted minority and rights groups.
The United Nations' top court also ordered the Myanmar government to prevent a repeat of the crimes, undertake legal reforms to protect the Rohingya, and provide the victims with reparations or, where it cannot, compensate them.
The judgment came seven years after The Gambia filed the case with the court in 2019, accusing Buddhist-majority Myanmar of a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder against the country's predominantly Muslim Rohingya community in 2016 and 2017.
It is the ICJ's first finding of genocide against a state, and the first ruling in any of the cases filed against Myanmar or its leaders in multiple courts around the world.

text:
Vietnam abolished the death penalty for drug trafficking and several other crimes on Friday, leaving execution available as a punishment for only four offences.
Communist Vietnam uses lethal injection as its execution method after retiring its firing squads in 2013, but has never made public the number of people it puts to death.
Amnesty International estimates more than 1,200 people were on death row in the country at the end of 2023.
In September, 11 people were condemned to die for trafficking drugs from France to Vietnam, according to media reports.
Under a revised penal code passed by the National Assembly on Friday, capital punishment will be available for only four crimes: treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production.
In addition to drug trafficking, the offences removed from the list included crimes against humanity, war crimes, rebellion and rape of a juvenile, with their maximum sentence replaced by life imprisonment.

Security forces arrived in the town, which sits in Babil province about 60km southwest of Baghdad and is also known as Jurf al-Nasr, on Friday. AFGHANISTAN – Four students at a religious school were killed and another two were wounded when an old mortar shell exploded in the western Afghanistan province of Farah, a police spokesman said on Nov 20.
Pupils in Farah’s Bakwah district had taken their noon break when they found the unexploded shell, provincial police spokesman Kalimullah Nangyal said.
“The students had transferred that into the madrassa where the younger students pressed the shell and then it exploded inside the madrassa, killing four and wounding two students,” Nangyal told AFP.
The students killed were aged between 10 and 16, the police said, and the wounded were taken to the central hospital.
More than 45,000 Afghans have been killed or wounded by explosive remnants of war and mines since Soviet troops withdrew in 1989, according to the United Nations Mine Action Service.

The number of people attempting to cross the Channel from Belgium to reach Britain has risen 400 per cent this year, the governor of the coastal province of West Flanders said Friday.
Belgium intercepted 570 people trying to set off from its coast between January and October this year, compared with 102 in the same period last year, according to governor Jurgen Vanlerberghe.
The vast majority seek to reach Britain but the governor said Belgian authorities also arrested 69 individuals accused of human trafficking - people 'looking to profit at the expense of others'.
Asylum seekers bound for the British coast often set off in boats from northern France since the crossing is the shortest to England but Belgium is seeing an increase even though its coastline is significantly further away from UK shores.

Several factors are responsible for a situation in which disputing parties often find themselves waiting for decades before their cases are settled. A shortage of judges, unclear rules, frequent court adjournments, and corruption at all tiers are just a few of the underlying causes. Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
- Published
A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.
This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.
A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.
Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.
His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.

text:
4.2-magnitude earthquake rattles Los Angeles area
An early-morning 4.2-magnitude earthquake rattled the Los Angeles area on Friday.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the earthquake struck about a half-mile north-northwest of Commerce, California, which is about 7 miles from downtown Los Angeles.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass posted about the quake on social media, saying it likely woke up many Angelenos.
"While unsettling, there are no immediate reports of damage or operational impacts, including at LAX," Bass wrote. "The LAFD and City teams will continue to monitor and update as needed."
People reported feeling the quake as far away as Lancaster, California, about 80 miles north of downtown L.A., and Poway, California, about 115 miles to the south, the USGS said.
Shortly after 5:30 a.m., the LA Fire Department provided an update that no significant infra/structure damage or injuries were noted. The spokesperson added that the LAFD Earthquake Mode is complete and normal operation

Sudan war fuels an invisible economy of survival
On a Friday night in the UK city of Leeds, a nurse taps “send”. Thousands of miles away, a phone buzzes in a courtyard in Omdurman, Sudan, and a ledger of trust begins to turn.
She does not think of this as economics. She thinks of it as family obligation - not as finance, and certainly not as policy. Yet the journey of that single payment, from a British bank account to a pot of lentils shared among displaced neighbours, is a map of how Sudan survives.
It is a journey across a collapsing currency. Before the war, a dollar bought roughly 600 Sudanese pounds. Last month it passed 10,000, and the currency is still sliding.
Shopkeepers have shuttered their stores rather than sell at a loss when the rate lurches overnight. Average incomes have fallen to levels last seen in 1992, while government revenues dropped from roughly 10 percent of GDP in 2022 to below five in 2024.

A Health Ministry statement said 18 ambulances were dispatched to the scene of the accident to search for survivors.
The state-owned Akhbar El-Youm newspaper earlier said 16 people had been killed and 17 others injured in the accident.

title: A Static Movement? Repression, Resilience, and Reinvention in Egypt’s Human Rights Field since 2013
summary: A Static Movement? Repression, Resilience, and Reinvention in Egypt’s Human Rights Field since 2013 Arab Reform Initiative
text:
Introduction
Since the 2013 coup d’état and the consolidation of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s rule, the human rights movement (HRM) in Egypt has sought to maneuver amid multiple constraints. Its scope of action has narrowed dramatically, as legal persecution, travel bans, asset freezes, and the forced closure of organizations have decimated what was once a vibrant field, especially in the aftermath of the 2011 Revolution. The movement has not disappeared, however. Instead, it has adapted, fragmented, and, in some cases, quietly reconfigured its methods and ambitions. This contribution aims to reflect on the tension between the external appearance of stasis – if not metastasis – and the often-invisible forms of resilience and reinvention that persist under authoritarian pressure.

ai_summary: This analysis examines how Egypt's human rights movement has adapted and persisted under increased state repression since 2013.

في الوقت الذي يتعامل فيه معظم الناس مع الزجاج والمعادن باعتبارها أشياء لا تصلح للأكل، كان الفرنسي ميشيل لوتوتو يرى فيها وجبة عادية، بل مصدر رزق أيضًا، بعدما اشتهر بتناول أشياء غريبة، بينها أجزاء من السيارات والدراجات وأجهزة التلفزيون، وصولًا إلى طائرة كاملة، في واقعة جعلته يدخل موسوعة جينيس للأرقام القياسية.

كيف اكتشف ميشيل لوتوتو قدرته على أكل الأشياء الغريبة؟
ولد ميشيل لوتوتو في فرنسا عام 1950، وعُرف بلقب «Monsieur Mangetout»، الذي يعني بالفرنسية «السيد الذي يأكل كل شيء»، بعدما بدأ في تناول مواد غير غذائية منذ طفولته.

text:
The majority of people who have spent time in a US prison or jail have, at one point in their lives, been a victim of a violent crime, according to a new study. Researchers with Just Safe, a victims’ advocacy non-profit, found that 84% of people who had been incarcerated reported being assaulted, shot or stabbed before their first time in jail or prison.
The report is based on a nationally representative survey of 20,000 Americans. Of those who have been incarcerated, half of them had been hurt by a caregiver as a child and one-third were victims of sexual or intimate partner violence.
Lenore Anderson, president of the Oakland, California-based Just Safe, said this type of research can push the public and elected officials to reframe the politics of crime. Instead of simply focusing on punishment, the findings show the necessity of bolstering trauma recovery resources.

text:
The Dangote refinery IPO, which concluded its share subscription last month, marks a breakthrough for African stock markets. The offer drew four million unique subscription applications, and the final number is likely to rise once pension fund subscriptions are included. This could put it on par with Aramco’s 2019 IPO, which had 5.1 million subscribers. The Dangote IPO has surpassed previous listings on the continent, such as Kenya’s Safaricom, which had 840,000 subscribers.
Dangote framed the offer as a “People’s IPO,” saying he wanted cooks, gardeners, and drivers to own shares. He set a target of 10 million retail investors. This was a deliberately bold goal, given that the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) has only 2.7 million active investors. The IPO did not reach 10 million, but its four million applications already exceed the exchange’s entire active investor base.
Bringing more than seven million Nigerians, completely new to investing, into the market in a short time span is difficult.

On 13 November, the UN General Assembly Third Committee considered an amendment to a draft resolution on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions.
The UN amendment text sought to replace “their sexual orientation or gender identity” with “any other considerations that make them at heightened risk of extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions”.

A long-lost oil painting bought for £20 in a charity shop has been identified as a 19th century landscape worth £20,000.
The vendor was browsing a high street shop in Bracknell, Berkshire, earlier this year and purchased it for the meagre sum as he liked the look of it.
But astonishingly, when he showed it to an auction specialist, they immediately thought it could be a rediscovered work by the celebrated Russian-Swiss artist Nicholas Chevalier.
Further research has confirmed it is indeed one of his paintings which had been missing for more than 160 years.
Chevalier's admirers included the British Royal Family and he accompanied Prince Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, on part of his world tour, documenting the journey through sketches and watercolours.
He later received commissions from Queen Victoria.

text:
The Federal Government and the Kaduna State Government have pledged stronger support for Nigeria’s creative industry, urging young people to turn their artistic talents into viable businesses capable of generating employment, attracting investment and boosting economic growth.
The Minister of Art, Culture and Creative Economy, Hannatu Musa Musawa, and Kaduna State Governor, Senator Uba Sani, made the commitment on Friday at the opening of the sixth edition of the Kaduna Fashion and Art Exhibition (KAFART), a three-day event in Kaduna.
Musawa, represented by the Curator of the National Gallery of Arts, Mrs Nana Hajara Tijjani, described the creative industry as a major economic asset that could contribute significantly to national development if properly harnessed.

The process involves heating the chunky vertebrae of the fish — which typically grow to 2 meters (6.6 feet) in length — to as much as 900 degrees Celsius (1,650 degrees Fahrenheit) and then grinding the charred bones into a powder that absorbs heavy metals and other pollutants.
"It's a sustainable, ecological form of carbon that does not require the felling of trees," said Galileu da Silva Pires, a biology teacher at the Jose Mota school in Manacapuru, a town on the Solimoes River, about 100 km (62 miles) west of Manaus. Stepping onto an island in western Japan, tourists squeal with joy at the sight of hundreds of fluffy rabbits, but few realise the land was once home to a secret chemical weapons factory for the country's Imperial Army.
Okunoshima -- also known as "Rabbit Island" -- has a perimeter of just four kilometres but welcomes thousands of snap-happy visitors attracted by its bunny population each year.

SEOUL, Nov. 20 (Yonhap) -- President Lee Jae Myung on Friday approved the appointment of Kim Jong-chul as new commissioner general of the Korean National Police Agency (KNPA), his office said.
Lee's approval came after a parliamentary committee adopted a report on Kim's confirmation hearing with bipartisan support earlier this week.
Kim will fill a post that has remained vacant for nearly two years since the former police chief was suspended from duty in connection with former President Yoon Suk Yeol's failed martial law bid in late 2024.
 The KNPA commissioner general can be appointed by the president without parliamentary consent following a confirmation hearing.

MELITOPOL, November 20. /TASS/. Russian electronic warfare (EW) operators in the Orekhov area are successfully fending off both Ukrainian FPV drones and fixed-wing attack unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), a senior EW operator from the 291st Motorized Rifle Regiment with the call sign Fokus, told TASS.
"Most often, of course, in our sector, in our area of operations, we are combating FPV drones and fixed-wing attack UAVs. As we’ve already mentioned, we’re intercepting FPV drones exceptionally well by jamming their communication channels. First, we intercept the video feed from the drone using one system, then, using another system, we directly target the receiver, thereby cutting off its communication with the operator. It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.
The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.
None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.

text:
UNHCR's operations in the Central African Republic (CAR) are built on protection through presence, the cornerstone of the humanitarian response. Amid volatile security conditions and the spillover of the crisis in Sudan, UNHCR also remains ready to respond to emergencies. Durable solutions are another top priority supporting the voluntary, safe, and dignified return of Central African refugees, their sustainable reintegration, and their contribution to national development. Together with the Government of CAR and its partners, UNHCR provides protection and multisectoral assistance to internally displaced people (IDPs) and refugees, including Sudanese and Chadian refugees, while promoting durable solutions for Central Africans returning home. Its work is aligned with national priorities: the National Development Plan, the National Strategy for Durable Solutions and the Solutions Support Platform established under the 2022 Yaoundé Declaration.

There is a dead plant on the wall in New Delhi’s Gallery Espace, in Sonia Mehra Chawla’s Emerald Leaf & Golden Fibre, a jute plant, Corchorus capsularis, pressed in Barisal district on September 6, 1809, and printed here many times its size. A barcode of the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh is stuck at the bottom, like a price tag.
The sheet comes from the herbarium of Francis Buchanan-Hamilton, the Scottish surgeon and botanist, and it is his name, as the man who collected it, that is printed on it. Whoever in Bengal showed him the plant, cut it and dried it has no name anywhere.
Mehra Chawla has hung two of her own framed etchings on top of the sheet, partly covering it.
The etchings are from The Golden Fibre, a triptych she has worked on since 2024, made from these old herbarium sheets, the leaves etched in solid brown and the collectors’ handwriting carried over. title: Gulf consortium starts work to repair Syria's main motorway
text:
A Gulf consortium has started work to rebuild Syria's main road network, Transport Minister Yarub Badr told The National, as the country becomes a focal point of regional plans to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
The consortium, composed of major Saudi, Qatari and Kuwaiti companies, has already dug up a section of the north-south motorway, known as the M5, south of Damascus, Mr Badr said. Lagos, Nigeria — In too many communities across our continent, a baby born with a cleft lip or palate is met with fear instead of a plan. Some families are told the child is cursed. Some mothers are even forced out of their homes. Yet a cleft is one of the most common and treatable conditions in medicine. A safe operation, done early, lets a child eat, speak and grow up with a bright future.
So when that child goes untreated, the problem is not biology. It is a sign that something is missing: the surgeon, the anesthetist, the nurse, the working operating room, the reliable electricity, the road to the right hospital. In this way, cleft is a bellwether for the strength of health systems overall.
Across sub-Saharan Africa, 93% of people cannot get safe, affordable surgery and anaesthesia when they need it, compared with under 4% in wealthier regions. In Ethiopia alone, roughly five million needed operations go undone each year.

In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib, during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.

title: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries to take on launch operations for Japan’s H3 rocket
summary: Transfer of the operations from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency will take part in stages and begin with the next launch.
text:
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) will transfer launch operations for the country’s flagship H3 rockets to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI), beginning with the next launch, science minister Yoshihiro Seki said Friday.
The H3 is a two-stage liquid-fuel launch vehicle jointly developed by JAXA and MHI. It experienced failures with its first unit in 2023 and the No. 8 unit in December last year, but has since achieved success in three consecutive launches, indicating a sufficient level of technical maturity.
The transfer will take place in stages, starting with the H3-22 configuration, which has two LE-9 liquid-fuel engines and two SRB-3 solid-fuel boosters. Among the rocket’s three configurations, the H3-22 has the strongest track record, with five of its seven launches having been successful.
JAXA will continue to conduct launch operations when newly developed components, such as an improved version of the LE-9 engine, are put into practical use, according to the ministry.
ai_summary: JAXA is transferring launch operations for its H3 rocket to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries following the vehicle's recent technical maturation.

A Vincent van Gogh painting has set a new record after selling for £145 million at a Sotheby's auction in New York.
At its first auction appearance, the painting Chataigniers en fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees) set the highest price a Van Gogh painting has sold for at auction and the second-highest for any artwork sold at Sotheby's.
Gustav Klimt's Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer holds that honour, sold a year ago at Sotheby's for £180 million.
The Dutch artist painted the landscape scene in the final two months of his life after being newly released from the psychiatric asylum of Saint-Rémy.
He had moved to a scenic village north-west of Paris, where Van Gogh was said to have experienced a powerful wave of optimism and energy that spilt out onto his canvases, making this period 'the most urgent and expressive period of his career', according to Sotheby's.

title: Kenya: Women Farmers Earn 18 Percent More Per Hectare Despite Smaller Farms, FTMA Evaluation Finds
summary: [Capital FM] Nairobi -- Women farmers participating in the Farm to Market Alliance (FtMA) programme earn more per hectare than their male counterparts despite farming smaller plots and facing greater resource constraints, according to a nine-year evaluation released in Nairobi.
text:
Nairobi — Women farmers participating in the Farm to Market Alliance (FtMA) programme earn more per hectare than their male counterparts despite farming smaller plots and facing greater resource constraints, according to a nine-year evaluation released in Nairobi.
The evaluation found that women generate an average of KES 82,494 per hectare in main-season revenue, compared with KES 69,833 for men, an 18% difference.
Female farmers in the network cultivate an average of 1.9 acres, compared with 2.8 acres for men. The findings also show that 45% of surveyed women have no formal education, compared with 26% of men.
The report, released at the FtMA National Stakeholder Forum 2026, highlights the gains made in connecting smallholder farmers to agricultural inputs, training and markets, while identifying persistent barriers to financing, mechanisation and market access.

The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya population in a brutal 2017 military crackdown that displaced more than 700,000.
The UN top court ruled on Thursday, by a 9–6 vote, that Myanmar’s crackdown on the Muslim minority amounted to genocide.
The ruling is considered historic because it is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court, and only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the crime had been committed.

SEOUL, Nov. 20 (Yonhap) -- The National Assembly passed a bill Friday calling for official recognition and welfare benefits for more victims of crackdowns on pro-democracy movements, marking the first time in 26 years such a bill moved past the parliament.
The Democratic Merit Act, proposed and largely pushed through by the ruling Democratic Party (DP), aims to recognize those who were killed, went missing or suffered injuries during two democratic movements in 1979 and 1987.
Under current law, only those involved in the May 18 pro-democracy movement in the southwestern city of Gwangju in 1980 and the April 19 democratic uprising in 1960 have been subject to official recognition by the government.

text:
Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said.
NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.

Researchers in the Netherlands have investigated how salt marshes withstand powerful storms using the world’s biggest wave machine.
As sea levels rise and storms become more powerful, salt marshes could play an increasingly important role in coastal protection. A crucial question is whether severe storms will wash away vegetation and sediment from salt marshes and reshape the coastline, or whether marshes can act as a barrier.
The Delta Flume, just outside Delft in the Netherlands, is a hydraulic testing facility with a concrete trough 300 metres long, 9.5 metres deep and 5 metres wide. At one end, four big pistons drive a wave board backwards and forwards, producing waves up to 4.5 metres high.
For the experiment, researchers transplanted intact sections of salt marsh into the Delta Flume and exposed them to waves of increasing power. After 21 hours of wave action, the surface had been eroded by an average of about 7mm.

Yesterday, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague ruled that Myanmar is responsible for having committed a genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority in 2017.
The case was a landmark – the first time that a state was held responsible for genocide, and only the fourth time since the Holocaust that an international court ruled that the legal threshold to prove genocide had been met.
Seven years after the case was brought by The Gambia, the ICJ’s judges ruled, by a margin of nine votes to six, that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar’s security forces against the Rohingya population in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

Dear British friends,

text:
South Africa has spent nearly 20 years putting waste laws and policies in place. The Waste Act of 2008 says creating waste must be avoided where possible. Reusing and recycling items should happen instead and garbage should be safely disposed of. Its purpose is to protect people's health and the environment.
The National Waste Management Strategy, revised in 2020, is the plan for putting these goals into practice. From 2021, new rules also made producers of paper and packaging responsible for managing their products after people use them.
But laws alone don't reveal how much plastic is being recycled - or not. One estimate suggests South Africa generated about 1.55 million tonnes of plastic waste in 2020 but recycled only 301,000 tonnes - which means that four out of every five tonnes of plastic end up as garbage.

KARACHI: The Sindh Cabinet on Thursday approved the release of Rs5.766 billion for the second phase of the Karachi Safe City Project, directing that the project be commissioned within 18 months to strengthen security infrastructure.
Phase-II of the Karachi Safe City project includes installation of over 2,300 cameras — 870 for general surveillance and 1,300 with Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) and facial recognition and 80 for traffic enforcement.
The overall plan envisages installation of nearly 10,000 cameras at over 2,000 locations across the city after completion of all phases.
Briefing the media after the meeting, Senior Minister Sharjeel Memon said that the cabinet approved the release of Rs5.766 billion for the second phase of the Karachi Safe City Project.

Published: | Updated:
Labor is right to close a super loophole Treasury expects will cost taxpayers $480 million over the next decade.
But can it please stop making villains out of the retirees who have used it up until now?
The loophole allows people to use their super to buy a product that will pay them an income for life, sometimes years before they retire.
When Centrelink later works out how much Age Pension they qualify for, it uses an assumed rate of return to value the investment.

text:
«زي النهارده».. وفاة سردار الجيش المصرى السير لي ستاك إثر اغتياله (20 نوفمبر 1924)
شهد المشهد السياسى في 1924 احتقانًا بين سعد زغلول، الذي كان رئيسًا للوزراء، والملك فؤاد، وكانت المسألة السودانية هي خلفية هذا المشهد،وكانت الجماهير في السودان تهتف بوحدة مصر والسودان، وتألفت حركة وطنية هناك داعمة لموقف سعد زغلول وهى حركة (اللواء الأبيض) بقيادة الضابط السودانى على عبداللطيف، وعلى إثر هذه الأزمة بين سعد زغلول، الذي رفض فصل مصر عن السودان من جانب وبين الملك والاحتلال من الجانب الآخر، قدم سعد زغلول استقالته للملك في 29 يونيو 1924 ورفضها الملك، لكن كان هناك حادث آخر هزّ مصر وبريطانيا معًا.
وكان وراء قبول الاستقالة الثانية لسعد زغلول في23 نوفمبر 1924 وهو اغتيال السير (لى ستاك) سردار الجيش المصرى وحاكم السودان آنذاك، ففى 19 نوفمبر 1924 خرج السردار (لى ستاك) من مكتبه بوزارة الحربية قاصدا بيته في الزمالك، فأطلق عليه خمسة أشخاص الرصاص وكانوا متربصين بشارع إسماعيل أباظة الذي تقع فيه وزارة التربية والتعليم ووزارة الإنتاج الحربي الآن وكان اسمه قديمًا (شارع الطرقة الغربية) فأصيب السردار بإصابات خطيرة

title: Anthropic shares close 17% above IPO price after volatile Nasdaq debut
text:
Anthropic shares closed 17 per cent above their offer price on their first day of trading, as an early rally in the world's largest initial public offering faded amid broader caution over artificial intelligence stocks.
The company behind the Claude chatbot opened on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $111.50, 34 per cent above its $83 IPO price, briefly giving it a fully diluted valuation of about $2 trillion.
The stock then pared back its gains to close at $97.17. That values the company at about $1.75 trillion on a fully diluted basis, or about $1.27 trillion on the shares now outstanding.
Anthropic, led by chief executive Dario Amodei, raised $81.3 billion by selling 980 million shares, and a further $26 billion through a private placement, bringing the total to $107.3 billion. The deal overtook SpaceX's $86 billion listing in June as the largest on record.

title: Egypt uncovers hundreds of effigies, jewelry in ancient middle-class cemetery
summary: Egypt uncovers hundreds of effigies, jewelry in ancient middle-class cemetery TRT Afrika
text:
Egyptian archaeologists have uncovered an ancient cemetery containing hundreds of coffins, gold tongues and jewelry that served middle-class residents in the northern province of Menoufia, the Tourism and Antiquities Ministry said.

text:
The Covid-19 pandemic not only delayed Census 2021 but also shook the very foundations of India’s statistical system. For the first time in over a century, a major health crisis made it impossible to send enumerators door to door. Yet the pandemic’s effects went far beyond postponement. It disrupted the Civil Registration System (CRS), undermined projections based on outdated baselines and revealed new vulnerabilities in India’s demographic record-keeping.
India’s CRS – which records births and deaths – is supposed to be a continuous complement to the decennial census. But during the pandemic, the system came under unprecedented stress. Despite widespread mortality during the waves of 2020–21, not all deaths were officially registered, particularly in rural areas. Independent studies suggested excess mortality far above CRS figures. Lockdowns disrupted normal reporting channels, creating delays in tabulation. Some states struggled to transmit data centrally.

text:
Nasa's Voyager 1 has phoned home from a staggering one light-day away, with a radio signal from the spacecraft taking exactly 24 hours to reach Earth. The historic transmission, received by flight controllers on Thursday, marks the first time a human-made object has communicated with Earth from this distance, after travelling more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometres) into interstellar space.
The confirmation, received on Thursday through Nasa's Deep Space Network, marks another landmark in the nearly 49-year journey of the spacecraft through interstellar space.
Voyager 1 crossed the one-light-day distance threshold on Wednesday at 5:16 am EST (10:16 GMT), Nasa said. The signal travelled at the speed of light before being received by antennas near Madrid, Spain, and relayed to the mission team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in California.

title: Scorpions sting and hospitalize hundreds in Egypt, roused by freak storm
summary: Scorpions sting and hospitalize hundreds in Egypt, roused by freak storm The Press Democrat
text:
Aswan, Egypt, is one of the world’s driest cities, where it hardly ever rains. Situated along the Nile River and home to more than 1.5 million people, it averages just 0.12 inches (3 millimeters) of rain per year.
But on Friday and Saturday, intense thunderstorms and even hail deluged the desert city and parts of the surrounding region. The Associated Press reported that the torrents caused flooding and power outages, closed schools and left three people dead.
The rains also unleashed something especially sinister: hordes of highly venomous scorpions whose stings hospitalized 503 people, according to Ehab Hanafy, undersecretary of the Health Ministry in Aswan.
Hanafy said the three deaths were “due to storm-related accidents” and “absolutely not because of scorpion stings.”

Ruff goodbye! Rolo the hospital therapy dog retires after 12 years on the ward
After 12 years of bringing joy to hundreds of hospital patients, Rolo the therapy dog is taking a well-earned retirement.
The springer spaniel cross poodle worked his last day at Ipswich Hospital in Suffolk on November 17, after completing 584 visits in his long career.
Rolo's heartwarming work comes after an incredibly tough start to life.
Just weeks before Christmas 2013, young Rolo was saved from 'certain death' at a puppy farm in South Ockendon, Essex.
Weighing just 2.5kg, he was rescued by the RSPCA alongside 29 other dogs.
Shortly after being rescued, Rolo became very sick, leading his carers to fear the worst.
But after some tender loving care, he recovered and was nursed back to health before being adopted at 12 weeks old.
Alongside his owner Claire Dean, Rolo joined Pets As Therapy in November 2014 and began a career in bringing some much-needed comfort to hospital patients.

- Published
The former principal of a daycare centre in Indonesia has been sentenced to five years in jail over the abuse and neglect of children in the unlicensed facility.
In April, a raid of the Little Aresha centre in the city of Yogyakarta exposed the culture of abuse within its walls â where toddlers were found with their hands and feet tied with rags.
